settings.heading: ABOUT THIS CHAPTER
settings.katha: Bengal’s river delta gave India its finest cotton. Muslin so sheer it was once said to be woven air came from these waters, and the habit of wearing soft, breathable cotton never left. Our East chapter begins with the cloth that carries that habit forward: mul cotton, light enough for a Kolkata summer and strong enough for daily wear.
settings.about: East India is humid, green and full of rivers, and its textile life grew around that climate. Cotton that breathes, spun fine and woven loosely, was the obvious answer. Mul cotton is the everyday descendant of that tradition. It is not a showy cloth. It is the one people reach for first, because it is soft on the skin, drapes without weight and gets better after every wash.

settings.heading: The landscape behind the loom
settings.paragraph_1: The Ganga and Brahmaputra meet the sea in the world’s largest delta. Warm, wet air favours fine cotton, and for centuries Bengal’s weavers worked near river ports, so cloth moved quickly from loom to market and from there across the world.
settings.paragraph_2: Fine cotton asks for patience. Yarn that is spun thin is fragile, and a weaver in a humid climate has a real advantage: damp air keeps the thread from snapping. Many of the traditional centres sit close to water for exactly this reason.
settings.paragraph_3: Today, mul cotton is woven and finished in several parts of the country, but its reputation still points east. It is the soft, plain-spoken cloth behind summer sarees, kurtas and shirts, and the base for stripes, checks and woven borders.

settings.title: MUL COTTON
settings.description: Mul, or mulmul, is the name for a very fine, soft, lightweight cotton. The word is tied to the muslin tradition of Bengal, where the thinnest yarns were woven into cloth that felt almost weightless. A good mul cotton has a close, even weave, a gentle crinkle after washing and a drape that falls rather than stands. It breathes in heat and layers easily in cooler months. In the house, mul cotton is used for sarees with woven stripe borders, for relaxed kurtas and shirts, for co-ord sets and for children’s clothes, where softness matters most. Look for an even surface, a cloth that softens with wear and borders that are woven in, not printed on.
settings.quote: Mul is the cloth you stop noticing, which is the point.

settings.title: BALUCHARI
settings.description: Baluchari is Bengal’s narrative silk. The pallu is woven as a set of framed scenes, often from the epics or from old court life, built up thread by thread with an extra weft on a jacquard loom. Bishnupur, a temple town known for its terracotta, is the centre of the craft today. Our Single Thread Baluchari keeps to one colour of figuring weft, so the pictures read like an engraving. Meenakari Baluchari adds small inlays of a second and third colour, the way enamel is set into gold.
settings.quote: The pallu is a picture book you can wear.

settings.title: SWARNACHARI
settings.description: Swarnachari is Baluchari’s festive sibling. The same framed scenes run across the pallu, but they are woven in gold or silver zari rather than silk, so the figures catch the light. Our Meenakari Swarnachari sarees add coloured highlights inside the zari, in the manner of enamel work, on deep red, green and blue grounds.
settings.quote: Baluchari tells the story; Swarnachari lights it up.

settings.title: Mul Cotton
settings.description: Stripes, thin checks and quiet woven borders. Designs stay minimal so the softness of the cloth leads.

settings.heading: Motif & colour
settings.subheading: Documented tendencies rather than rules. Weavers have always adapted these to taste, trade and occasion.

settings.text: Hold it to the light. Real mul is fine and even, with soft slubs here and there, not stiff or glossy.
Wash a swatch or read the care label. Good mul cotton softens and crinkles a little. Cloth that stays stiff after washing may be heavily starched.
Look at the border. A woven stripe shows on both sides of the cloth, where a printed one sits only on the surface.
Ask for the fibre content. Pure cotton breathes and absorbs sweat, blends do not behave the same way.
Expect small irregularities. A tiny slub or a slightly uneven stripe is part of handwoven cloth, not a defect.

settings.heading: How to spot the real thing
THE FUTURE OF THESE CRAFTS
settings.paragraph_1: Mul cotton is one of the most practical textiles India makes, and it suits a warming climate. The craft is not fading so much as being asked to do more, with more garment types, more colours and more everyday uses.
settings.paragraph_2: What helps most is honest labelling and fair prices. Fine yarn and careful weaving take time, and a price that respects that keeps the looms working.
